messages.body_plain:
Hi
I'm planning a distance sampling survey for a tropical forest bird species (Príncipe Thrush - Turdus xanthorhynchus) and am wondering what type of rangefinder to use . Distances likely to be in the region of 5-30 meters. Does anyone have a preferred rangefinder model? Would a basic golf/hunting model like this be suitable www.amazon.co.uk/TACKLIFE <https://www.amazon.co.uk/TACKLIFE-Continuous-Magnification-Measurement-Waterproof/dp/B07H3JS5L1/ref=sr_1_5?keywords=rangefinder&qid=1556790370&s=gateway&sr=8-5>?
Cheers
Frazer

Dear experts

Birdlife Denmark is doing national abundance estimates for all common birds species based on line transect counts. We are hoping to get some advice or maybe verification, that we are doing the analyses appropriately.

We are conducting the analyses in R with the distance-package.

Study design very briefly (I can elaborate if necessary):

Approx. 1500 transects of 1 km evenly spaced in Denmark in which the observer recorded perpendicular distance to each individual in four distance bins, 0-25 m, 25-50 m, 50-100m, above 100 m. Unfortunately we do not have information on group size or behavior for the observations.

Explanation of the variables:

-          Sample label: transect id

-          Distance: the distance bin of each individual (recorded as 24, 49, 99)

-          Effort: 1 km (transect length)

-          Area: surface area of Denmark in square km

-          Species: the species at hand

-          Stage: we did three transect counts in each transect (early spring, late spring, winter). We hope to produce national estimates for each species for each of the three stages.

-          Euring: an ID number that is unique for each species

-          A number of habitat variables that describe the amount of each type of habitat in quarters (noted by the observer on the first count in the transect). We choose to work with the aggregated habitat variable “open_habiat”

We are running 5 different models for each species and choosing models based on AIC. The 5 models are:

Three simple keyfunctions as detection function:

1.      1 Uniform with cosine adjustment.

2.      2 Half normal (“hn”) with no adjustment terms.

3.      3 Hazard rate (“hr”) with no adjustment terms

Two functions with added covariable: the amount of open habitat registered by the observer recorded in quarters (0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 or 1) to account for different detectability in the transects.

4.      4 Half normal with amount of open habitat as covariable

5.      5 Hazard rate with amount of open habitat as covariable

Below is an example of the line of code that we are using in R. It corresponds to model 5 in the above section.

dist.bins <- c(0,25, 50, 100)

ds(blue_tit_data, formula= ~ open_habitat, cutpoints=dist.bins, convert.units=0.001, key="hr", adjustment=NULL)

Daniel

Your interpretation is generally correct.  Here are a few comments:

you provide no goodness of fit for your model.  I'm guessing this is because you have no degrees of freedom remaining from your binned data after fitting a 3-parameter hazard rate model with a covariate
the effect of the covariate seems marginal based on the relative magnitude of the point estimate of the coefficient -0.06 and the SE of that coefficient 0.06.  I presume the sign of the covariate effect (negative) goes the "right way":  greater cover shrinks the sigma parameter (decays detection more rapidly)
the convert.units argument trips up many people, but you've done that correctly.
density estimate is 23 birds per square kilometer, and the size of the study area is 42895, making total abundance the product of these two quantities: just about a million birds.  Confidence interval on the abundance estimate ranges from 906.7 thousand to 1076.0 thousand birds.  I think the confidence interval is a preferable way to report precision rather than standard error (but that is personal preference).
I presume for blue tits lacking information on group size is not problematic as they are likely to be detected as singles, but this may be a bigger problem for other species
you could do some further "sense checking" that your results are sensible by asking whether it is plausible that at distances of 40m you are likely to miss 4 of 5 blue tits
assuming the duration of the "early survey" is a few weeks, you would state that "the size of blue tit population in Denmark averaged 987.762 thousand..." with the given levels of precision.  Surveys that are undertaken over a period of time estimate the average of the population over the duration of the survey

I can't guarantee the differences you are seeing between dsm in R and DSM in Distance 7.3 are the result of data formatting issues, but that seems a good place to start.

For an example of data organisation for the R package dsm, have a look at the Gulf of Mexico spotted dolphin vignette on our website: http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/mexico-analysis.html

- `segdata` containing information (including covariates) for **all** segments (with or without detections)
- `distdata` with information about the detections (group size, perpendicular distance, etc)
- `obsdata` describing segments in which detections were made.

No need for NAs.  There is also a `preddata` data object describing covariates in each cell of the study area, for use in prediction

Thanks for sending along your data.  I gave your data this treatment for detection function fitting and model selection:

library(readxl)
martins <- read_excel("dsmartes2.xlsx",
                      col_types = c("numeric",
                                    "text",
                                    "numeric",

                                    "numeric"))

                    "Effort", "Region.Label", "Area")

martins <- as.data.frame(martins)

hncos <- ds(martins, transect="point",
               key="hn", adjustment = "cos")
hnherm <- ds(martins, transect="point",
            key="hn", adjustment = "herm")
hrcos <- ds(martins, transect="point",
            key="hr", adj="cos")
hrherm <- ds(martins, transect="point",
            key="hr", adj="herm")
restable <- summarize_ds_models(hncos, hnherm, hrcos, hrherm)
knitr::kable(restable)
plot(hrcos, pdf=TRUE)

It seems there is little effect of adjustment terms upon model performance.  Your data are lumped, likely because of measurement error I would guess.  But I would speculate that the key function likely captures the essence of the process giving rise to your data.

I suspect you need to think about the estimates the analysis produces, if it is camera trapping data.  Because the units of effort are not lengths but rather times, there might need to be another transformation the estimates undergo before being actual density or abundance estimates. Hi Emiliano,

On the comment Eric made about unit of effort being time, if I understand correctly the general point of relevance here will apply to all camera trap studies, and is that you can't infer density directly from data about moving animals detected on cameras. What these data tell us about is better termed something like 'activity', which is an amalgam of density (number of individuals) and movement (levels and distribution) of these individuals. The value of carrying out distance analysis is that you should be able to express activity in terms of the number of animals that intersect an area of standardised size per unit time (e.g. animals per ha per hr). If you wanted to derive density in the surrounding area from these data, I think you would have to combine them with some kind of movement model describing the distance and spatial configuration of movements of individuals in the wider area. If I sound a bit vague about this it's because I have never done it before! However, lots of relevant analytical methods have been developed. A good place for you to start, if you are not already familiar with these, might be here:

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/aje.12557

Best of luck,

Mark

messages.body_plain:
I believe it is possible to estimate absolute density from camera trap data,
although there is a correction needed for proportion of animals not moving if
you can't sample at a time of day when this proportion is negligible.  A recent
paper by Eric Howe provides in introduction in the distance sampling context:

Howe et al. 2017. Distance sampling with camera traps. Methods in Ecology and
Evolution
https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12790

(There are also papers by Marcus Rowcliffee cited there that take a different
approach.)

with a follow-up

Howe et al. 2018. Model selection with overdispersed distance sampling data. MEE.
DOI: 10.1111/2041-210X.13082

Spatial capture recapture may also be an option for some studies:

Despres-Einspenner et al. 2017 An empirical evaluation of camera trapping and
spatially explicit capture‐recapture models for estimating chimpanzee density.
Am J. Primatology. https://doi.org/10.1002/ajp.22647

Cheers, Len

On 17-May-19 12:15 PM, Mark Wilson wrote:
> Hi Emiliano,
>
> On the comment Eric made about unit of effort being time, if I understand
> correctly the general point of relevance here will apply to all camera trap
> studies, and is that you can't infer density directly from data about moving
> animals detected on cameras. What these data tell us about is better termed
> something like 'activity', which is an amalgam of density (number of
> individuals) and movement (levels and distribution) of these individuals. The
> value of carrying out distance analysis is that you should be able to express
> activity in terms of the number of animals that intersect an area of
> standardised size per unit time (e.g. animals per ha per hr). If you wanted to
> derive density in the surrounding area from these data, I think you would have
> to combine them with some kind of movement model describing the distance and
> spatial configuration of movements of individuals in the wider area. If I sound
> a bit vague about this it's because I have never done it before! However, lots
> of relevant analytical methods have been developed. A good place for you to
> start, if you are not already familiar with these, might be here:
>
> https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/aje.12557
>
> Best of luck,
>
> Mark

Yes, for Eric Howe's method you need to chunk the data up into "snapshots" with
effort for each camera being the number of snapshots.

I believe that Marcus Rowcliffe's approach instead incorporates assumptions
about animal movement; there is also recent work by Richard Glennie along these
lines that isn't yet in print but is avalable on his web site
http://www.richardglennie.co.uk/
(direct link to manuscript http://www.richardglennie.co.uk/files/moveds.pdf).
Richard's work is not aimed at camera trapping specifically, but more generally
at tackling the problem of movement in distance sampling.  Nevertheless there is
a bit in that paper about point transects that could be useful for camera
trapping studies.

Hope this is all useful, Len

My name is Irene and I am a PhD student who is planning, with my colleagues in Ecuador, a distance sampling survey of spider monkeys in a tropical forest. Does anyone have been estimating distances in similar conditions and have a preferred range finder model? All recommendations/suggestions are more than welcome.

Also, another researcher, Frazer Sinclair, asked a similar question some days ago. Would you be able to share your answers to his question (if any)?

Thank you in advance!

Best regards,

Irene

The cause of the error is that Distance requires a field in the shape file attributes called LinkID, populated with numerical values.  In your case, with only a study area layer, that number would be 1.

There is a section in Chapter 5 of the Users Guide, entitled "Importing GIS Data by Copying an Existing Shapefile
into the Data Folder" where this field is described:

> Open the newly renamed shapefile in your GIS package, and add a field to the table. The field should be able to contain long integer numbers – in ArcView this means the field type should be “Number”, the width 16 and decimal places 0. Name this field “LinkID”.
> • The LinkID field will be used to link records in the shapefile to records in Distance’s internal data table for this layer. Each
> LinkID value must correspond with a value in the ID field of Distance’s internal table.
> • If you only just created the Data Layer in Distance, then it doesn’t matter what order you number the records in the LinkID field of the shapefile. Start with 1, and go up to the number of records you have.

A better option is to download the newest version of Distance, 7.3.  This version includes a new shape file import utility that  simplifies bringing shape files into Distance.
